export const meta = {
  name: 'samsung-tri-vendor-correspondence',
  description: 'Three-way command-level correspondence across Extron ControlScript, Extron .pkp and Crestron CCD for one Samsung display; design the IR',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Anatomy', detail: '8 parallel analysts over the Crestron JSON, IR package, Extron module and .pkp' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'adversarial skeptic per dimension, re-checking against the files' },
    { title: 'Synthesize', detail: 'IR design + emission feasibility + completeness critic' },
  ],
}

const R = '/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert'
const S = `${R}/samples/Samsung QNxxLS03DAFXZA`
const O = `${R}/tools/out/crestron`

const GROUND = `
THE SAMPLE: one physical device — a Samsung QN43LS03DAFXZA "The Frame" style display —
with drivers from BOTH major control-system vendors. This is a natural experiment: two
independent teams encoded the same device protocol, so differences are representational,
not behavioural.

FILES (quote paths with spaces):
  Extron ControlScript module (serial):
    "${S}/controlscript/smsg_display_QNxxLS03DAFXZA_Series_v1_0_0_0.py"   (16,346 bytes)
    "${S}/controlscript/smsg_display_QNxxLS03DAFXZA_Series_v1_0_0_0.pdf"  (comm sheet)
  Extron Global Configurator package:
    "${S}/pkp/smsg_10_6738_v1_0_0.pkp"    "${S}/pkp/smsg_10_6738_v1_0_0.pdf"
  Crestron Certified Driver packages (from Crestron's first-party driver site):
    "${S}/Crestron/Serial/FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial.pkg"
    "${S}/Crestron/IP/FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_IP.pkg"
    "${S}/Crestron/IR/FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_IR.pkg"

ALREADY ESTABLISHED BY DIRECT INSPECTION THIS SESSION (verify if it matters to you, but do
not waste effort re-deriving):

A) Extron .pkp = gzip -> .NET BinaryFormatter (NRBF) stream, unencrypted/unsigned. A WORKING
   PARSER EXISTS at ${R}/tools/pkp_dump.py — it gunzips a .pkp, walks every record, and emits
   JSON. Use it: 'python3 ${R}/tools/pkp_dump.py <file.pkp> -o out.json'. The .pkp embeds the
   complete GC-runtime Python driver as bytes in a StreamResourceAsset keyed by filename, plus
   DriverCommandAsset / EnumParamAsset / DecimalParamAsset / EnumStateAsset / DriverModelAsset
   metadata. EnumStateAsset._tag holds wire tokens; DecimalParamAsset carries _min/_max/_suffix.

B) Crestron .pkg = a plain ZIP. Members:
     Serial: <name>.dat (15,308 B JSON) + <name>.dll (62,624 B .NET assembly)
     IP:     <name>.dat (52,476 B JSON) + <name>.dll (99,488 B .NET assembly)
     IR:     <name>.ir (2,648 B) + <name>.dat (16,908 B JSON) + <name>.pdf   — NO DLL
   Already extracted to ${O}/{Serial,IP,IR}/.

C) The outer .dat JSON is a CAPABILITY MANIFEST — manufacturer, deviceTypeId, supportedModels
   (146 entries), inputs, a 63-entry 'features' list of Supports* booleans, communication
   defaults (RS232 9600 8N1), connections, userAttributes. It contains NO wire commands.

D) The REAL driver definition is embedded inside the DLL as PLAIN UTF-8 JSON (not compressed).
   Already extracted to:
     ${O}/Serial_embedded_driver.json   (46,155 B)
     ${O}/IP_embedded_driver.json       (80,877 B)
   Top-level keys: SchemaVersion, GeneralInformation, UserAttributes, Transports,
   SupportedFeatures, CommandIds, Commands, Responses, Conditions, Transformations, Rules,
   Controllers, InputOutput. Serial has 50 Commands / 28 Responses / 15 Transformations /
   12 Rules / 14 Controllers; IP has 77 / 22 / 16 / 42 / 23.
   The DLL's own metadata names 'Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Core.LegacyWrappers' and the class
   'Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Legacy.<name>_dll', and the JSON carries "Type": "Simpl" — strongly
   suggesting the DLL is a thin shell around this JSON rather than hand-written device logic.

E) THE HEADLINE: at the wire level the two vendors AGREE BYTE FOR BYTE.
     Extron  SetVolume:    self.build(0x01, 0x00, 0x00, int(value))     (module line 204)
     Crestron SetVolume:   Function = "{:hex} 01 00 00 {Volume}"
     Extron  UpdateVolume: self.build(0xF0, 0x01, 0x00, 0x00)           (module line 211)
     Crestron GetVolume:   Function = "{:hex} f0 01 00 00"
   Crestron composes framing via templates: Command "Packet" wraps Function as
   "{:hex} 08 22 {Function}", and "PacketWithCheckSum" appends a Twos-complement Checksum
   transformation. Extron's self.build() does the same framing in Python.

RULES:
- Cite file path + line number, JSON path, or byte offset for every claim. No citation, no finding.
- Where the two vendors differ, the DIFFERENCE is the finding — do not smooth it over.
- You have Bash, python3, grep. For .NET DLL inspection try: monodis, ikdasm, ilspycmd, strings.
  If a tool is unavailable, say so rather than guessing at IL contents.
- Do NOT write anywhere under ${R}/tools/ (another process owns it) — work in /tmp.
`

const FINDINGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    summary: { type: 'string', description: '4-8 sentences' },
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          evidence: { type: 'string', description: 'path:line, JSON path, or byte offset' },
          confidence: { type: 'string', enum: ['high', 'medium', 'low'] },
          bearing: { type: 'string', enum: ['crestron-in', 'crestron-out', 'ir-design', 'both', 'neither'] },
          implication: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'evidence', 'confidence', 'bearing'],
      },
    },
    openQuestions: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'summary', 'findings'],
}

const VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    verified: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['CONFIRMED', 'REFUTED', 'UNCERTAIN', 'OVERSTATED'] },
          note: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'verdict'],
      },
    },
    missedOrWrong: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'verified'],
}

const DIMS = [
  {
    key: 'crestron-schema',
    prompt: `Reverse-engineer the COMPLETE SEMANTICS of Crestron's embedded driver JSON schema from
${O}/Serial_embedded_driver.json and ${O}/IP_embedded_driver.json.

For each top-level section — Transports, SupportedFeatures, CommandIds, Commands, Responses,
Conditions, Transformations, Rules, Controllers, InputOutput, UserAttributes — document every
distinct object shape, every "Type" discriminator value observed, and what each field means.

Pay special attention to the composition model: Commands of Type "Template" reference another
command by CommandName and supply Values; Type "Text" supplies literal Content with {Placeholder}
substitution; Transformations (Checksum, AsByte, Slice, ...) post-process. Work out the full
evaluation order that turns a high-level SetVolume into wire bytes, and write it down as an
algorithm someone could implement.

Do the same for the response side: RootProcessingNode -> CommandResponseDecoders -> named decoders,
the "Next" chaining, "Processing": "Stop", match types (AlwaysMatch, CommandResponseNameMatch, ...).
Explain how a received byte sequence is routed to a feedback value.

Enumerate every "Type" value you see across the whole file so the schema's vocabulary is captured
rather than sampled. This document is the foundation everything else depends on — be exhaustive
and precise.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'crestron-serial-vs-ip',
    prompt: `Diff the Crestron Serial driver against the Crestron IP driver for the SAME device
(${O}/Serial_embedded_driver.json vs ${O}/IP_embedded_driver.json).

The IP driver is substantially larger (77 vs 50 Commands, 42 vs 12 Rules, 71 vs 12 InputOutput
entries). Establish exactly what the extra material is and why: is it a richer protocol, an
authentication/pairing handshake, additional feedback, media-service/app control, or schema
evolution (Serial sdkVersion 21 vs IP sdkVersion 14 per the outer .dat)?

Build the command-name diff both ways. For commands present in both, are the wire payloads the same
(Samsung's IP protocol differs from its serial protocol, so establish whether the Function bytes
match or diverge)? Compare Transports config, UserAttributes (4 vs 12 — what extra config does IP
demand?), and the Configuration section that only IP has.

The point of this dimension: determine whether ONE device yields ONE logical driver with N transport
bindings, or genuinely N independent drivers. That decision shapes any intermediate representation.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'crestron-ir',
    prompt: `Analyze the Crestron IR package, which is the interesting outlier: it has NO DLL at all
(members are .ir + .dat + .pdf), so it must be fully declarative.

Files under ${O}/IR/. Determine the .ir file format (Crestron IR files are a documented-ish binary
format — establish its structure: header, function-name table, per-function timing data / carrier
frequency / burst pairs). Establish what the .dat manifest declares differently from the Serial and
IP manifests, and note that its outer .dat reported sdkVersion 22.0000.0000 and
supportedPlatforms ["4-Series"] with inputCommandsFriendlyNames.

Then answer the question that matters: IR is one-way with no feedback, so how does the manifest
express that, and what does the absence of a DLL prove about when Crestron requires compiled code?
If IR drivers need no DLL, the DLL is carrying the command/response engine binding — test that
hypothesis against the evidence.

Also extract the list of IR function names and compare them to the Serial driver's command names.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'crestron-dll',
    prompt: `Determine what the Crestron .dll actually CONTAINS beyond the embedded JSON — this
decides whether "Crestron in" is a JSON-extraction problem or a decompilation problem.

Files: ${O}/Serial/*.dll (62,624 B) and ${O}/IP/*.dll (99,488 B), both PE32 .NET assemblies.

The embedded JSON is 46,155 B of the 62,624 B Serial DLL — about 74%. Account for the REST. Is the
remaining IL a thin generated wrapper (a class deriving from a LegacyWrappers base that just loads
the resource), or is there real device logic? Enumerate the types and methods in each assembly.

Try monodis, ikdasm, ilspycmd, or 'dotnet-ildasm' if present; if none are installed, try
'pip install pythonnet'-free approaches — a minimal PE/CLI metadata reader in Python over the
#~ and #Strings heaps is entirely feasible and is the right fallback. Report the TypeDef and
MethodDef name lists.

Answer decisively: can a converter get 100% of the driver's behaviour from the embedded JSON alone,
or is some behaviour only in IL? Check both DLLs, since IP may differ from Serial. Also determine
whether the assembly is strong-name signed or Authenticode signed, since that bears directly on
whether third parties can produce loadable packages.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'extron-samsung',
    prompt: `Analyze the Extron side of this Samsung device: the ControlScript module at
"${S}/controlscript/smsg_display_QNxxLS03DAFXZA_Series_v1_0_0_0.py" and the .pkp at
"${S}/pkp/smsg_10_6738_v1_0_0.pkp".

Run the existing parser: python3 ${R}/tools/pkp_dump.py "<the .pkp>" -o /tmp/samsung.json
Extract the embedded GC Python from the StreamResourceAsset and compare it to the shipped
ControlScript module, exactly as was done for the Extron first-party devices.

IMPORTANT: the repo owner states this .pkp covers BOTH serial and IP for this display. Verify that
— look for multiple ProtocolAsset entries (EthernetProtocolAsset and any serial equivalent) and for
multiple DriverModelAsset entries. If one .pkp really does carry two transports while Crestron ships
two separate .pkg files, that is a first-class structural difference between the vendors and is
central to the IR design. If it does NOT, say so plainly and correct the owner.

Also: this is a THIRD-PARTY device (Samsung, not Extron), so it tests the earlier finding that the
Extron toolchain's ### BEGIN AUTO GENERATION structure and SIS-specific handshake were Extron-only.
Report whether this non-SIS driver uses the same generator markers, the same BaseDriver subset, and
what replaces the SIS 'w0echo/w3cv' handshake and the E## error-code table. This is the single most
valuable thing this dimension can establish.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'three-way-commands',
    prompt: `THE CENTRAL DELIVERABLE. Build the complete three-way command correspondence table for
this Samsung display across:
  (A) Extron ControlScript module  "${S}/controlscript/smsg_display_QNxxLS03DAFXZA_Series_v1_0_0_0.py"
  (B) Crestron Serial driver JSON  ${O}/Serial_embedded_driver.json
  (C) Crestron IP driver JSON      ${O}/IP_embedded_driver.json

For EVERY command in each, resolve it down to the actual wire bytes it produces. On the Extron side
that means reading self.build() and each Set*/Update* method and expanding the framing. On the
Crestron side that means evaluating the Template composition chain (Packet -> PacketWithCheckSum)
including the checksum transformation.

Produce a table with one row per logical capability: Extron command name, Extron wire bytes,
Crestron command name, Crestron wire bytes, MATCH / DIFFER / EXTRON-ONLY / CRESTRON-ONLY, and notes.

Then do the same for FEEDBACK: Extron's AddMatchString regexes vs Crestron's Responses decoder tree.
Are the response patterns recognising the same byte sequences?

Quantify: what percentage of capabilities appear in both, and of those, what percentage produce
byte-identical wire traffic? A verified number here is the empirical foundation for the whole
project — get it right and show your working. Where the two disagree on bytes, investigate whether
one is wrong or they are addressing different device firmware.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'ir-design',
    prompt: `Design the manufacturer-neutral INTERMEDIATE REPRESENTATION, grounded in this specific
three-way sample rather than in the abstract.

You now know both sides concretely: Extron encodes commands as Python methods that build byte
strings plus regex match strings; Crestron encodes them as composable JSON command templates with
named transformations plus a response-decoder tree. Both ultimately describe: framing, a per-command
payload, parameter substitution and typing, checksums, and a response grammar.

Specify the IR concretely — actual schema, with field names and types — covering: device identity
and supported models; transport bindings (and how ONE logical driver carries multiple transports);
capability/command set with parameters, types and ranges; wire encoding as composable templates
(since Crestron's template model is strictly more expressive than a flat command string, consider
adopting something like it); transformations (checksum algorithms, encoding, slicing); the response
grammar; state/feedback mapping; and vendor-specific escape hatches.

Critically, TEST YOUR DESIGN: walk at least 5 real commands from the sample — including SetVolume,
a discrete input select, a power command with warmup/cooldown semantics, a polling command, and one
that exists on only one side — through IR and back out to BOTH vendor formats. Show where it works
and where it leaks. Name what your IR cannot represent.

Also address: Crestron declares a fixed deviceTypeId taxonomy ('FlatPanelDisplay') and a 63-entry
Supports* feature list; Extron has no such concept. Does the IR need a capability taxonomy, and if
so whose?`,
  },
  {
    key: 'crestron-emission',
    prompt: `Assess CRESTRON-OUT concretely, now that the format is known: what would it take to
GENERATE a loadable Crestron .pkg from an Extron driver?

Mechanically the package is a zip of {manifest .dat, driver .dll}. The manifest is plain JSON and is
clearly generatable. The hard part is the DLL. Establish: could a generator produce the DLL by
TEMPLATING — taking a known-good Crestron DLL, swapping the embedded JSON resource, and rewriting the
type name — rather than compiling C# from scratch? Assess how feasible that is given .NET assembly
structure (resource sizes and offsets, metadata heaps, strong-name signature if any). Test the idea
as far as you can with the actual files.

Alternatively: what would compiling from source require — which Crestron SDK reference assemblies,
what target framework, is the SDK publicly downloadable or gated?

Then the acceptance question, which dominates: is a .pkg validated, signed or certified before a
processor will load it? Look for signature blobs in the DLLs, signing metadata in the manifest
(the manifest has 'developer', 'developerContact', 'licenseRequired', 'driverId' GUID), and any
integrity hash. Use the Bright Data CLI ('brightdata search' / 'brightdata scrape') for Crestron SDK
documentation on loading and side-loading drivers — NOT WebFetch/WebSearch, and never curl to target
sites, as the machine owner's home IP must not be used for crawling.

Give a blunt verdict with the single hardest blocker named.`,
  },
]

phase('Anatomy')
log('Three-way analysis: Samsung QN43LS03DAFXZA across Extron ControlScript, Extron .pkp, and 3 Crestron CCD packages')

const analyzed = await pipeline(
  DIMS,
  (d) => agent(`${GROUND}\n\nYOUR DIMENSION: ${d.key}\n\n${d.prompt}`, {
    label: `anatomy:${d.key}`, phase: 'Anatomy', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA, model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high',
  }),
  (res, d) => {
    if (!res) return null
    return agent(
      `${GROUND}\n\nYou are an adversarial verifier for dimension "${d.key}". REFUTE the findings below rather than ` +
      `agreeing with them. Open the files and check each claim yourself. CONFIRMED only if you personally reproduced ` +
      `the evidence; REFUTED if contradicted; OVERSTATED if directionally right but claimed too strongly; UNCERTAIN ` +
      `if uncheckable.\n\nBe most skeptical about: claimed byte-level equivalences (expand the templates and checksums ` +
      `yourself), percentage figures (recount them), and any claim that something is "fully declarative" or "thin ` +
      `wrapper" without having actually enumerated the IL.\n\nAlso report what was MISSED.\n\n` +
      `Their brief:\n${d.prompt}\n\nTHEIR FINDINGS:\n${JSON.stringify(res, null, 2)}`,
      { label: `verify:${d.key}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA, model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
    ).then((v) => ({ dimension: d.key, analysis: res, verification: v }))
  }
)

const dossier = analyzed.filter(Boolean)
const counts = dossier.reduce((a, d) => {
  for (const v of (d.verification && d.verification.verified) || []) a[v.verdict] = (a[v.verdict] || 0) + 1
  return a
}, {})
log(`${dossier.length}/${DIMS.length} dimensions done — ${JSON.stringify(counts)}`)

phase('Synthesize')
const EV = JSON.stringify(dossier, null, 2)

const [verdict, critic] = await parallel([
  () => agent(
    `${GROUND}\n\nVerified evidence dossier from 8 dimensions, each adversarially checked, follows.\n\n` +
    `Write the STRATEGIC SYNTHESIS. Treat REFUTED as false, OVERSTATED as weaker, UNCERTAIN as unproven.\n\n` +
    `Structure:\n` +
    `1. What this one sample proves that the earlier Extron-only work could not. Lead with the strongest ` +
    `empirically-verified statement about cross-vendor correspondence.\n` +
    `2. Crestron IN — verdict and method, now that the driver definition is known to be JSON.\n` +
    `3. Crestron OUT — verdict, the DLL problem, and the acceptance/certification blocker.\n` +
    `4. The IR: adopt one, or not? If yes, its shape in a page, and the specific things it cannot hold.\n` +
    `5. What the product actually is. Consider seriously that the right artifact may not be a "converter" ` +
    `at all but a device-protocol database with N emitters — argue it out rather than assuming.\n` +
    `6. The honest risk list and what remains unproven.\n` +
    `7. Concrete next steps, ranked, including exactly which additional sample files would most reduce uncertainty.\n\n` +
    `The reader is an AV professional who writes code. Prose with headings, minimal bullets, cite evidence, ` +
    `no padding. Do not hedge where the evidence is clear; do not overclaim where it is not.\n\nDOSSIER:\n${EV}`,
    { label: 'synthesis:tri-vendor', phase: 'Synthesize', model: 'fable', effort: 'max' }
  ),
  () => agent(
    `${GROUND}\n\nDossier from 8 dimensions follows.\n\nYou are the COMPLETENESS CRITIC. Do not summarise. ` +
    `Identify what remains unanswered, which claims survived only because nobody checked them, which files were ` +
    `never opened, and where dimensions CONTRADICT each other. Pay particular attention to whether the headline ` +
    `byte-level correspondence claim was actually verified across the full command set or generalised from a ` +
    `handful of examples.\n\nThen give a prioritised list of what to obtain or do next, ranked by uncertainty ` +
    `removed per unit effort. Be blunt.\n\nDOSSIER:\n${EV}`,
    { label: 'completeness-critic', phase: 'Synthesize', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
  ),
])

return { dimensions: dossier.length, verdictCounts: counts, dossier, verdict, completenessCritic: critic }

analysis.summary: The Crestron embedded driver JSON is a rule-engine DSL, not a command list: a high-level state-machine (Controllers) drives named Commands (Text | Template | WakeOnLan) that compose via {Placeholder} string substitution and post-process via named Transformations, gated by Rules (Block/CommandSequence/SequencedEntry/SetOtherOnSend/SetOtherState/SetOtherFeedback) evaluated against boolean Conditions (IsEqual/IsMatch/Exists/And/Or). Responses are decoded by walking a tree of named nodes from a transport's RootProcessingNode through CommandResponseDecoder -> CommandResponseNameMatch (correlate to the outstanding request name) -> a payload matcher (Regex/BinaryPacket/Json/AlwaysMatch/bare-Select leaf) that extracts placeholders and runs Transformations to write state, with "Processing":"Stop" pruning siblings and Next arrays doing depth-first fan-out/chaining. Serial and IP share the identical vocabulary (Type discriminators are the same across both transports) but IP adds JSON-RPC command bodies keyed by an AccessToken/CommandId auth handshake, HTTP status/JSON-error interception (CheckHttpResponseCode, JsonResponseErrorCheck ConditionType:"Ack"/leaf "Nak"), and compound Conditions (And/Or/Exists) that Serial never uses. The wire-level byte-for-byte match with Extron noted in the prompt is visible directly in Commands[Name=SetVolume]/[Name=Packet]/[Name=PacketWithCheckSum] in Serial (lines 384-448). This document treats every object as fully enumerated from the two supplied files; no field or Type value was sampled and skipped.

findings.evidence: Serial_embedded_driver.json:384-401 (PacketWithCheckSum) and :413-429 (SetVolume)
findings.claim: Command Type=Text with an Info.Content template plus a Transformations array is the base 'compose a string, then post-process pieces of it' primitive: PacketWithCheckSum's Content is literally '{Body}{CheckSum}', and its own Transformations compute CheckSum from the as-yet-unresolved {Body} placeholder (via Checksum then AsByte) before the final string is assembled.
findings.failure_scenario: A converter that treats Transformations as 'run after the whole command string is built' rather than 'run per named placeholder before it is substituted into the parent Content' will compute the checksum over the wrong (already-checksum-appended) byte range and emit a wrong trailing checksum byte.

findings.evidence: Serial_embedded_driver.json:403-412 (Packet) and :413-429 (SetVolume referencing CommandName=Packet)
findings.claim: Command Type=Template has Info={CommandName, Values}: it does NOT build wire text itself, it looks up the named command (here 'PacketWithCheckSum'), and supplies Values as a dict of placeholder-name -> template-string that get substituted into named holes of the referenced command's Content (recursively, since Template can reference another Template, e.g. SetVolume->Packet->PacketWithCheckSum).
findings.failure_scenario: Flattening Template.Values directly into the leaf Text.Content by name-matching alone (ignoring the CommandName chain) breaks any driver where the same placeholder name is reused at two different levels with different meanings, or where a Template's Values itself contains further {Placeholder} tokens that must be resolved bottom-up.

findings.evidence: Serial_embedded_driver.json:384-429 (PacketWithCheckSum, Packet, SetVolume chain)
findings.claim: Full composition/evaluation order for SetVolume->wire bytes, derived by tracing Commands[SetVolume]->Commands[Packet]->Commands[PacketWithCheckSum]: (1) start with SetVolume.Info.Values={Function:'{:hex} 01 00 00 {Volume}'}; (2) run SetVolume.Transformations: AsByte({Volume}) writes the numeric Volume state as a little-endian byte, overwriting the {Volume} binding; (3) substitute into Function -> resolved byte string; (4) climb to referenced command Packet, whose Values={Body:'{:hex} 08 22 {Function}'} -- substitute the resolved Function into Body; (5) climb to PacketWithCheckSum, whose Content='{Body}{CheckSum}' -- first run ITS Transformations: Checksum({Body})->CheckSumAsString, AsByte(CheckSumAsString)->CheckSum; (6) substitute Body and CheckSum into Content to get the final wire bytes. The '{:hex}' prefix token marks the following space-separated pairs as literal hex-byte constants (as opposed to a placeholder substitution) -- it is a formatting sigil consumed at the leaf, not itself a Transformation.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer who evaluates Transformations only at the top-level command (SetVolume) and not also at the nested leaf (PacketWithCheckSum) will send a packet with a garbage/zero checksum byte, since the checksum-computing Transformation lives on the leaf command, not the caller.

findings.evidence: Serial_embedded_driver.json:958-965 (RootProcessingNode), :1005-1020 (CommandDecoderDefault Processing:Stop)
findings.claim: Response decoding is a tree walk starting at the Transport's named ResponseProcessor (Transports[0].ResponseProcessor='RootProcessingNode'). RootProcessingNode (Type=AlwaysMatch) fans out unconditionally to Next=[CommandResponseDecoders, ConsumeUnusedBufferData] -- i.e. both children are always attempted, in array order, unless a prior sibling's node carried "Processing":"Stop" and matched, in which case remaining siblings in the SAME Next array are skipped (seen at CommandDecoderDefault and every PollResponseDecoder, all of which set Processing:Stop before their own Next chain runs).
findings.failure_scenario: Implementing Next as 'first match wins, stop' globally (rather than only when the matched node itself declares Processing:Stop) would incorrectly stop the tree before ConsumeUnusedBufferData ever gets a chance to run on non-command-shaped bytes, or would incorrectly prevent AlwaysMatch fan-out nodes like RootProcessingNode/CommandResponseDecoders from trying every branch.

findings.evidence: Serial_embedded_driver.json:966-978 (CommandResponseDecoders dispatch) and its CommandResponseNameMatch children e.g. PowerPollCommandDecoder Match:'GetPower'
findings.claim: CommandResponseDecoders (Type=CommandResponseDecoder) is a dispatch node whose Next list is a set of CommandResponseNameMatch children (PowerPollCommandDecoder, VolumePollCommandDecoder, ...) each carrying a Match regex tested against the NAME of the command currently outstanding/awaiting a response (not against the received bytes) -- e.g. Match:'GetPower'. This means response routing is keyed by 'what did we just send', and only after that lookup does control pass to a byte-pattern node (Regex/BinaryPacket/Json) that actually parses the payload.
findings.failure_scenario: A stateless response parser that tries to match incoming bytes against BinaryPacket templates without first knowing which command is outstanding will get false matches/misses, because several poll responses (Power/Volume/Mute/Channel/Input/VideoConfiguration) differ only in a single byte at a fixed offset (Function ID: 00/01/02/03/04/05) inside an otherwise identical envelope, and the schema resolves that ambiguity via the outstanding-command name, not by payload shape alone.

findings.evidence: Serial_embedded_driver.json:1081-1097 (PowerPollResponseDecoder) vs the near-duplicate PowerPollResponseDecoder2 immediately following, both under PowerPollCommandDecoder.Next
findings.claim: BinaryPacket response nodes use the same '{:hex} <bytes> {Placeholder}' template mini-language as command Text/Template Content, but as a MATCH pattern instead of a build pattern: literal hex bytes must match exactly, and each {Placeholder} captures raw bytes into a named variable (e.g. PowerPollResponseDecoder captures {Data1}{Data2}{Data3}{CheckSum} from the tail of the packet) which downstream AlwaysMatch response nodes (GetPowerResponse etc.) then feed through named Transformations to produce final state values. Two near-duplicate decoders exist for the same poll: PowerPollResponseDecoder expects a doubled preamble '{:hex} 03 0c f1 03 0c f5 08 f0 00 00 00 f1...' while PowerPollResponseDecoder2 expects the same without the leading '03 0c f1' echo, both feeding the same GetPowerResponse leaf.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer who only encodes one of these two BinaryPacket variants will silently drop power feedback whenever the device happens to echo (or not echo) the query bytes before its reply -- a device-timing quirk the driver authors clearly hit and special-cased.

findings.evidence: Serial_embedded_driver.json:1043-1056 (AckResponseDecoder->GetAckResponse, GetAckResponse has no Type key); IP_embedded_driver.json:1441-1450 (SetAccessTokenToNull, Nak -- also no Type key)
findings.claim: A response node lacking a 'Type' key entirely (e.g. GetAckResponse, and IP's Nak/SetAccessTokenToNull) is a distinct, valid leaf shape: it carries no Match/payload-matching logic of its own and is reached purely by being listed in a parent's Next array after that parent already matched; its own job is just to run Select (literal/extracted state writes) and/or resolve a named Condition via 'ConditionType':'Ack' (e.g. GetAckResponse: ConditionType=Ack, Condition=IsAck, and IP's CheckHttpResponseCode: ConditionType=Ack, Condition=Http200).
findings.failure_scenario: A schema reader that requires every Responses[] entry to have a 'Type' field (to route it through one of AlwaysMatch/Regex/BinaryPacket/Json/CommandResponseDecoder/CommandResponseNameMatch handling) will throw or silently skip these Ack/Nak/Select-only terminator nodes, breaking ACK/NAK resolution for every Set command (Serial CommandDecoderDefault->AckResponseDecoder->GetAckResponse) and the IP unauthorized-access recovery path (JsonResponseErrorCheck->Nak, UnauthorizedAccessCheck->SetAccessTokenToNull).

findings.evidence: IP_embedded_driver.json:351-357 (RpcRequest), :358-365 (WakeOnLan), :373-380 (GetAccessToken)
findings.claim: IP's RpcRequest Text command embeds an unresolved literal brace inside its own template via doubled braces: Content='{{"method":"{method}","params":{"AccessToken": "{AccessToken}", {params}},"id":{_CommandId_},"jsonrpc":"2.0"}}' -- i.e. the templating engine must distinguish '{{' / '}}' as literal JSON braces from single '{Name}' as a placeholder, and must also support a leading-underscore namespace ({_CommandId_}, {_MacAddress_}) that resolves against CommandIds/UserAttributes rather than Controllers-managed state.
findings.failure_scenario: A naive regex-based placeholder substitution that treats every '{...}' span (including doubled braces) as a placeholder name to look up will fail to parse RpcRequest/RpcPollRequest/GetAccessToken's literal JSON structure, either throwing on an unrecognized key or corrupting the JSON-RPC envelope; separately, treating {_CommandId_} as a normal state name (looked up in Controllers) rather than the CommandIds MonotonicIntegerId generator will send a wrong/static id and break request/response correlation for the JSON-RPC transport.

findings.evidence: IP_embedded_driver.json:1234-1241 (RootProcessingNode, no Type key) vs Serial_embedded_driver.json:958-965 (RootProcessingNode, Type=AlwaysMatch)
findings.claim: IP's RootProcessingNode omits an explicit 'Type' key (unlike Serial's, which has Type:AlwaysMatch) yet behaves identically -- proving 'Type' on a fan-out node is optional and defaults to always-evaluate-every-child-in-order, and that Type is a behavior discriminator applied per-node-kind, not a schema-required field.
findings.failure_scenario: A parser requiring 'Type' on every Responses[] entry, or assuming absence of 'Type' always means 'Ack/Nak leaf' (as it does at Serial's GetAckResponse), will misclassify IP's RootProcessingNode as a leaf and never dispatch to CheckHttpResponseCode/JsonResponseErrorCheck/CommandResponseDecoder, silently dropping all IP feedback.

findings.evidence: IP_embedded_driver.json:1477-1484 (NoAccessToken Condition), :2071-2079 (RequireAccessToken Rule), :1429-1445 (UnauthorizedAccessCheck->SetAccessTokenToNull)
findings.claim: IP layers an authentication state machine on top of the same Rules vocabulary Serial uses for simpler gating: Conditions[NoAccessToken] (Exists, Invert=true) drives Rules[RequireAccessToken] (Block on Send, Except='GetAccessToken') so every command except the token request itself is held until an AccessToken exists; Rules[StartTimerWithAccessTokenCommand] (SetOtherOnSend, sets AccessTokenBlocker=true) plus Conditions[AccessTokenBlockerTimerInEffect] and Rules[BlockAccessTokenRequest] throttle re-requesting the token; and Responses[UnauthorizedAccessCheck] (Json, Condition=Unauthorized, Next=[SetAccessTokenToNull]) resets AccessToken to a sentinel 'unknown' on a -32010/-32700 JSON-RPC error, which re-triggers NoAccessToken and restarts the flow. This entire login/refresh cycle has NO counterpart anywhere in the Serial driver (Serial has no Conditions of Type Exists, no AccessToken state at all) -- it exists purely because the IP transport is a stateless per-request JSON-RPC/HTTP call requiring a session token, whereas Serial is a persistent byte stream needing none.
findings.failure_scenario: A generic cross-transport driver abstraction that assumes 'the same Rules types produce the same behavior on both transports' will miss that IP's Block/SetOtherOnSend/Condition combination implements a full auth-token lifecycle (acquire, gate-all-else, expire-on-401-equivalent, backoff-retry) that must be reproduced exactly for IP control to work at all, while a Serial implementation with the identical Rule types wired differently only has to handle power-gating and channel-entry debouncing.

Having done the diff myself: it is ALL of the first three, not just schema evolution. Evidence: GeneralInformation.MinSdkVersion is '21.0000.0000' in Serial_embedded_driver.json vs '14.0000.0000' in IP_embedded_driver.json (schema evolution, confirming the outer .dat's 21-vs-14 split), but the command-name diff shows genuinely new capability classes unique to IP: JSON-RPC media/app control (GetAccessToken, RpcRequest, RpcPollRequest, GetFirstScreenApp/SetFirstScreenApp, GetMultiViewModes/SetMultiViewMode1-3, RemoteKey, WakeOnLan), and TV-tuner/antenna config (SetAnalogAirAntenna, SetAnalogCableAntenna, SetDigitalAirAntenna, SetDigitalCableAntenna, SetAntennaTemplate, SetTvInput, SetTvPlus) plus picture/sound presets (SetPictureModeDynamic/Filmmaker/Movie/Standard, SetSoundModeAmplify/Standard) and display rotation (SetDisplayRotatorControlLandscape/Portrait). Command-name diff (computed directly from the two Commands arrays): 44 shared names, 6 Serial-only (GetVideoInput, Guide, Packet, PacketWithCheckSum, SetPowerOn, ToggleMute), 33 IP-only (listed above plus GetArtwork, GetPower2, GetReportedVideoInput, Return, ForwardScan, ReverseScan, SetMute). 44+6=50 (matches Serial's Commands length) and 44+33=77 (matches IP's), so the counts reconcile exactly.

The brief explicitly asked whether Function bytes match for commands present in both drivers — they do NOT, and this is the single biggest finding the stub findings entirely missed. Serial commands use a proprietary binary hex-packet template (CommandName: 'Packet'/'PacketWithCheckSum', payload e.g. SetVolume: '{:hex} 01 00 00 {Volume}', GetPower: '{:hex} f0 00 00 00', ChannelUp: '{:hex} 0d 00 00 12' — Serial_embedded_driver.json, Commands entries named SetVolume/GetPower/ChannelUp). IP commands with the SAME NAME use a completely different wire protocol: JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTPS (CommandName: 'RpcRequest'/'RpcPollRequest'), e.g. SetVolume -> method 'directVolumeControl' with params '"volume":"{Volume}"'; GetPower -> method 'powerControl'; ChannelUp -> method 'channelUpDnControl' with params '"control":"channelUp"' (IP_embedded_driver.json, Commands entries named SetVolume/GetPower/ChannelUp). So for every one of the 44 shared command names checked (SetVolume, GetVolume, SetPower, GetPower, GetMute, ChannelUp, ChannelDown, SetChannel, GetChannel, SetVideoInput, GetVideoConfiguration, SetVideoConfiguration, SetMediaService, SetArtwork), the Serial and IP payload encodings diverge completely — same command taxonomy/naming, wire-incompatible bodies. This directly contradicts an extrapolation of the sample brief's 'Extron and Crestron agree byte-for-byte' finding (which was Extron-serial vs Crestron-serial only) onto Serial-vs-IP: it does NOT hold across transports for the same vendor's own two drivers.

IP requires a real authentication/pairing handshake that Serial has no equivalent of, which the stub findings never surfaced. Evidence: IP_embedded_driver.json Commands.GetAccessToken sends {"method":"createAccessToken","id":"{_CommandId_}","jsonrpc":"2.0"}; every subsequent RpcRequest/RpcPollRequest template embeds "AccessToken": "{AccessToken}" in its params. IP_embedded_driver.json Rules contains 'RequireAccessToken' (Type: Block, blocks all commands except GetAccessToken when condition NoAccessToken) and 'BlockAccessTokenRequest' (rate-limits token re-requests) — Serial_embedded_driver.json Rules has no AccessToken-related rule at all (its NeedsPowerOn Except-list has no '.*AccessToken.*' clause, unlike IP's, which does). IP's UserAttributes (12 entries) also encode a real pairing/config requirement absent from Serial (4 entries): a mandatory 'MacAddress' Custom attribute (RequiredForConnection: Before, used for Wake-on-LAN) plus explicit end-user instructions to accept an on-screen 'Allow' pairing prompt on the TV during driver load ('Configuration Instructions 2' / 'Enable Instructions' description) and to pre-provision four DefaultXxxChannel attributes for tuner sources. This is a genuine device-side authorization step, not just 'more config fields.'

UserAttributes 4-vs-12 is explained concretely, not left as an open question: the 8 extra IP attributes are MediaServiceConfiguration guidance, the MAC-address requirement + WOL notice (IP powers on via Wake-on-LAN, per SetPower using method 'powerControl' with no serial-style dedicated SetPowerOn command — note Serial's SetPowerOn is Serial-only, confirming Serial and IP use structurally different power-on strategies: Serial has a Rules-driven CommandSequence 'SendPowerOn' -> SetPowerOn per Serial_embedded_driver.json Rules[1], while IP relies on WakeOnLan as a distinct IP-only Command), the pairing-prompt instructions, a Multiview-naming caveat, and four Default*Channel attributes for tuner-source presets. This is IP-specific real-world deployment friction, not schema noise.

Transports differ structurally in a way the stub findings missed entirely: Serial_embedded_driver.json Transports[0] is Type 'Serial' with TimeBetweenCommands 250ms, WaitForResponseTimeout 1000ms, no auth. IP_embedded_driver.json Transports[0] is Type 'Http', posting to 'https://{_Host_}:{_Port_}' with ContentType application/json, Secure: true but HostVerification/PeerVerification both false (TLS with certificate validation disabled — a security-relevant detail worth flagging), Timeout 8s. These aren't parameter variants of one transport model; they are different transport types entirely (serial byte stream vs. HTTPS JSON-RPC client).

IP-only 'Configuration' section (absent from Serial) was not examined by the stub: it contains exactly one key, 'DriverInstanceIdentifier': '{_MacAddress_}' (IP_embedded_driver.json, top-level 'Configuration') — the driver instance is keyed by MAC address, consistent with the WOL/pairing model above.

Scope mismatch that bears on the brief's central question (one logical driver vs N independent drivers): Serial's GeneralInformation.SupportedSeries lists 4 series ('LS Series', 'QN85D', 'Neo QLED QN90D Series', 'QN95D') and OtherSupportedModels has >140 entries spanning multiple product years, while IP's SupportedSeries is only 'LS Series' and OtherSupportedModels has 23 entries, all within the LS/Frame family. So the IP driver is narrower in device-model scope but wider in feature/command surface for the models it does cover — i.e., the two files are not simply 'the same logical device, N transports': IP encodes Frame-specific smart-TV/art-mode/app features that may not even apply to the broader panel lineup Serial claims to support. This argues AGAINST a naive single-logical-driver-with-transport-bindings IR and for treating feature availability as transport-and-model-conditional.

analysis.summary: The Crestron IR package (FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_IR.pkg) has no DLL because it needs none: the .ir file is a fully self-contained, flat binary blob (2,648 bytes, fully parsed with no trailing garbage) built from a single repeated TLV record scheme — [total_len byte][tag/id byte][payload] — holding a header (model/manufacturer/date/category strings), a 41-entry function-name table (id 1-41 -> "Power_On".."Select"), and 41 corresponding pre-recorded IR waveform blocks in the same id order, keyed by the same ids. There is no command grammar, no response parsing, no checksum/transform pipeline, and no state to hold — a 4-Series processor just looks up a name and blasts the matching byte blob out the IR port. The outer .dat manifest structurally confirms this: it has no assemblyFileName/className keys at all (Serial and IP both declare these, pointing at their .dll and its Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Legacy.* class), no userAttributes/extensionDeviceData, and a communication block that is just {"type": "Ir"} versus Serial's full RS232 property block and IP's port/isServer block. Feedback is expressed by omission, not by a false flag: the IR features array has 26 entries (vs 63 for Serial/IP) and the entire Supports*Feedback vocabulary (SupportsFeedback, SupportsPowerFeedback, SupportsMuteFeedback, SupportsInputFeedback, SupportsChannelFeedback, SupportsVolumePercentFeedback, SupportsAudioInputFeedback, SupportsVideoInputFeedback, SupportsDisconnect, SupportsReconnect, etc.) is simply absent — not set to false, not present. This supports the hypothesis directly: the Serial/IP DLLs exist to carry the Commands/Responses/Conditions/Transformations/Rules engine (parsing bytes back off the wire, computing checksums, mapping states), and IR has none of that machinery in its JSON schema (no Commands/Responses/Rules keys at all in the .dat), so no compiled engine is needed — DLLs appear exactly where response/composition logic exists, and disappear exactly where it doesn't.

analysis.summary: Both DLLs are pure thin wrappers — there is no device logic in the IL at all, only PE/CLI plumbing wrapped around the embedded JSON resource. Each assembly's #~ metadata tables contain exactly two TypeDefs (the compiler-generated <Module> and one driver class) and exactly one MethodDef: a 22-byte-IL constructor that does nothing but call System.Type.GetTypeFromHandle(self) and pass that plus a hardcoded resource-name string literal to an external base-class constructor (Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Core.LegacyWrappers.DisplayWrapperSerial for Serial, DisplayWrapperTcp for IP). There are zero Field rows and only two MemberRefs (GetTypeFromHandle, base .ctor). The ~74%/81% of file size "beyond the JSON" is not code — it is PE/COFF headers, CLR metadata tables/heaps, a native Win32 version resource (.rsrc, 832B/816B), a boilerplate .reloc stub (12B), and (appended outside the mapped sections) a 1184-byte Authenticode WIN_CERTIFICATE block. A converter gets 100% of the device-specific behavior from the embedded JSON manifest resource alone — there is no hidden IL logic to decompile in these two files. The real protocol interpreter (whatever code evaluates "Rules"/"Transformations"/"Conditions") lives entirely in the external, not-shipped Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Core assembly (referenced only as an AssemblyRef, v26.0.0.0 for Serial / v24.0.0.0 for IP), so understanding the JSON schema's runtime semantics is a schema-interpretation problem, not something recoverable from these package files at all. Neither DLL is strong-name signed (COR20 Flags=0x1, StrongNameSignature RVA/Size=0/0), but both carry an Authenticode PKCS#7 block signed by a self-signed "Crestron Electronics Inc / Firmware Department" certificate (subject==issuer, 1024-bit RSA/SHA-1, serial 0x132b66c, artificial 100-year validity 2010–2110) — the identical certificate/serial in both files, meaning it is a fixed internal signing key baked into Crestron's driver-build toolchain rather than a CA-chained trust signature.

analysis.summary: Extron's serial module and Crestron's Serial driver JSON encode the identical MDC-style wire protocol: same 6-byte body (08 22 cmd1 cmd2 cmd3 value) plus the same two's-complement checksum, verified computationally for every shared command. Of the 8 capability families Extron exposes (AspectRatio, AudioMute, ChannelStep, Input, Keypad, MenuNavigation, Power, Volume), all 8 have a Crestron-Serial correspondent (100% coverage on Extron's side), and of those, 6 are fully byte-identical, 1 (AspectRatio) is byte-identical on its two shared enum values but Extron has an extra "Custom" value Crestron lacks, and 1 (ChannelStep) genuinely DIFFERS — Extron uses a dedicated command family (0x03) while Crestron emulates a remote-key press (0x0D .. 0x12/0x10) for the same user-facing action. That's 6/8 = 75% full match, 87.5% match-or-partial, 12.5% true byte divergence among shared families. Feedback: Extron's 4 AddMatchString regexes and Crestron's 4 corresponding terminal response decoders (Power/Volume/Mute/Input) recognize byte-for-byte identical response-frame prefixes, but Crestron's Power decoder also accepts a 0x08 data byte that Extron's regex character class omits. Crestron-Serial additionally exposes 8 capability families entirely absent from Extron (direct channel tuning, app launch, transport controls, color keys, Guide, Art Mode, Ambient Mode, dash key) — these are CRESTRON-ONLY, not disagreements. The Crestron IP driver is a categorically different protocol: JSON-RPC over what is Samsung's SmartView/remote-control API (human-readable methods like "powerControl"/"directVolumeControl", string params, an AccessToken auth handshake) with zero byte-level relationship to the MDC hex frames — it is not "wrong," it targets the TV's network control surface rather than RS-232, and it exposes a still-larger capability superset (50+ named streaming apps, PictureMode, SoundMode, DisplayRotator, MultiView) that neither serial driver can reach at all.

findings.claim: ChannelStep is the one genuine wire-level disagreement between Extron and Crestron-Serial for a capability both vendors claim to support: Extron sends a dedicated 'channel step' command family (cmd1=0x03), Crestron emulates a remote-control keypress (cmd1=0x0D, value 0x12 up / 0x10 down).

If the device firmware only implements one of the two mechanisms, one vendor's channel-step feature is silently non-functional on this unit.

findings.claim: The Crestron-IP driver is not a byte-comparable dialect of the same protocol — it is Samsung's JSON-RPC 'SmartView' remote-control API (AccessToken handshake, human-readable methods like 'powerControl'/'directVolumeControl'/'remoteKeyControl', string values 'powerOn'/'powerOff') with zero structural relationship to the 08-22-prefixed MDC hex frames used by Extron and Crestron-Serial.

Neither driver is 'wrong' — RS-232 MDC and the network SmartView API are genuinely different transports Samsung ships on the same panel.

findings.claim: Extron's response regexes hardcode the response frame's trailing checksum byte as a literal small enumeration when the value-space is small (Mute: values {0,1} paired to checksum bytes {0x11,0x10}; Power: values {0,4,5} paired to {0x13,0x0F,0x0E}) but wildcard the checksum byte entirely when the value-space is large (Input: 5 values, checksum wildcarded [\x00-\xFF]; Volume: 101 values, checksum wildcarded), whereas Crestron's BinaryPacket decoders always capture the checksum generically as a named field ({CheckSum}) and never verify it against the body.

But idx15 (PowerPollResponseDecoder2) has a shorter, DIFFERENT prefix ('03 0c f5 08 f0 00 00 00 f1', missing the leading '03 0c f1'), which is not 'the same prefix' as Extron's and represents an additional acceptance path Extron has no equivalent for at all. The 0x08-value nuance (MapPowerFeedback Transformations[9]: '\b'(0x08)->false) is correctly identified, but lumping idx14/idx15 together as 'same prefix' understates that Crestron's power-feedback matching is more permissive than Extron's in two independent ways, not one.

verified.claim: Extron regexes hardcode checksum as enumeration where value-space is small (Mute, Power) but wildcard it where large (Input, Volume); Crestron never verifies checksum
verified.note: Verified the four AddMatchString regex literals directly (lines 38-41): Mute checksum class [\x11\x10] (2 values), Power [\x13\x0F\x0E] (3 values), Input and Volume both wildcard [\x00-\xFF]. Crestron Responses[14]-[20] all end in a bare {CheckSum} capture with a SubstringRemoveLastByte transform and no arithmetic verification step, confirming the 'never verifies' half. One nuance the finding doesn't surface: because the data-byte character class and checksum-byte character class are independent regex alternations (not jointly constrained pairs), Extron's 'enumeration' actually accepts several non-corresponding data/checksum combinations too (e.g. for Power, 3x3=9 combinations match, only 3 of which are arithmetically valid) — so even the 'enumerated' cases aren't true checksum verification, just per-byte allow-lists. This is broadly consistent with the finding's own 'fakes verification' framing, so I don't consider it a refutation, just an under-explored detail.

The headline 'union of 16 families, 8/16=50% shared' statistic mixes families of very different internal size (9-command MenuNavigation and 10-command Keypad counted the same as 1-command Guide/Dash) — presented with the same certainty as the more rigorous, like-for-like 6/8 and 7/8 figures, but it is a much softer, methodology-dependent number that wasn't flagged as such.

Extron's checksum formula `(~sum(command_string) & 0xFF) + 1` has a latent, code-only edge case: when sum%256==0 the expression evaluates to 256, and `bytes([256])` would raise ValueError in real Python (not wrap to 0x00 as Crestron's twos-complement would). This never triggers for any command in this driver (verified: no real command body sums to a multiple of 256), so it doesn't affect the correspondence table, but it's a code-level asymmetry between the two vendors' checksum implementations that a fully rigorous 'byte-identical arithmetic' claim should acknowledge exists in principle.

Extron's 'enumerated checksum' regexes for Mute/Power don't actually pair the data byte with its correct checksum (the two character classes are independent alternations), so they accept several arithmetically-invalid data/checksum combinations — a slightly different characterization than 'enumeration as verification' implies, though it doesn't contradict the finding's own 'fakes verification' framing.

analysis.summary: The IR is a document with nine top-level sections — DriverDescriptor, Transports, Parameters, Templates, Transformations, Commands, ResponseGraph, StateModel(Controllers)/Rules/Conditions, and CapabilitySet/VendorExtensions — built by generalizing Crestron's own JSON shape (Serial_embedded_driver.json), since it is already a strict superset of Extron's flat build()+regex model: Templates are composable nodes (a Command references a parent "Packet" template which references "PacketWithCheckSum", mirroring Crestron's own Command→Template→Template chain), Transformations are named reusable pipeline steps (Checksum/Map/Math/Slice/Replace/Format), and the ResponseGraph is a decoder tree, so Extron's flat regex+callback list becomes leaf-only trees while Crestron's multi-stage decoders keep their branching. Walking five real commands (SetVolume, SetInput, SetPower with warm-up/cool-down, GetVolume polling, and Crestron-only SetArtwork) through the design forced two schema corrections mid-test: Command.templateRef must be transport-scoped, because Crestron's own Serial vs IP SetVolume use unrelated wire encodings for the identical logical command; and a boolean/enum command's wire frame can be value-dependent at the whole-template level, not just at one byte inside a shared template — Crestron's own SetPower/SetPowerOn split shows the "On" branch of SetPower's own substitution map is dead code, silently overridden by a Rule. The single largest asymmetry is warm-up/cool-down and command-guarding state machinery (Controllers, Rules, Conditions, PostCommandDelay): it is fully present and load-bearing in Crestron's JSON, and completely absent — not merely unused, structurally absent, confirmed in both the .py module and the .pkp packaging metadata — on the Extron side, so IR→Extron for that behavior is lossy by construction unless codegen synthesizes new imperative Python with no vendor-native counterpart. On the capability-taxonomy question: Crestron's deviceTypeId/63-flag Supports* list is real but partly aspirational (it declares SupportsSetAudioInputSource with no backing command), so the IR should treat capability flags as a derived projection computed from the command/state graph, with the flag vocabulary itself borrowed from Crestron's (the only side that has one) but kept open rather than owned by either vendor. Five vendor-specific behaviors — the SIMPL/DLL shell wrapper, GC's per-model .pkp asset duplication, IR's checksum-validation condition, Crestron's SequencedEntry channel-entry rule, and Extron's raw byte-2-tuple enum tables — have no natural IR-native slot and are pushed into a per-node VendorExtensions bag.

findings.claim: Concrete IR top-level schema (informal): DriverDescriptor{id, manufacturer, deviceClass, baseModel, driverVersion, supportedModels:ModelBinding[]}; ModelBinding{modelName, transportRefs[]}; Transport{name, kind:'serial'|'tcp'|'http'|'ir', responseRootRef, timing:{timeBetweenCommandsMs, waitForResponseTimeoutMs}, medium:{...kind-specific}}; ParamDef{name, type:'enum'|'integer'|'decimal'|'string'|'boolean', min?, max?, step?, unit?, enumValues?:{logical:wireBytesOrString}}; Template{name, kind:'literal'|'composite', parentTemplateRef?, values?:{placeholder:stringWithNestedRefs}, content?}; TransformDef{name, kind:'checksum'|'map'|'math'|'slice'|'replace'|'format', info:{...}}; Command{name, direction:'set'|'get'|'event', paramRefs:[], templateBindings:{transportRef:templateRef} (NOT a single templateRef — see finding below), valueTemplateMap?:{value:templateRef} (for value-dependent whole-frame selection), transformSteps:[{transformRef,input,output}], postCommandDelayMs?, statesSet?:[], ruleRefs?:[]}; ResponseNode{name, kind:'binaryPacket'|'regex'|'alwaysMatch'|'commandNameMatch', match?, select?, transformSteps?, output?, next?:[], terminal?:{conditionType,condition}}; Controller{name, type:'boolean'|'enum'|'numeric'|'string'|'timedStatus', pollingIntervalMs?, ackAsFeedback?, allowFeedback?, requireAck?, requireFeedback?, feedbackHoldoffMs?, deviceProcessingTimeMs?, commandRetryCount?, range?:{min,max,step}, rampingScheduleMs?:[], timedStatus?:{timeoutMs,minTimeoutMs,supportsChangeTimeout}}; Rule{name, appliesTo(regex), except?(regex), conditionRef?, type:'block'|'commandSequence'|'setOtherOnSend'|'sequencedEntry', info:{...}}; Condition{name, type:'isEqual'|'isMatch', invert?, values:{stateRef:literalOrPattern}}; CapabilitySet{deviceTypeId?, declared:{flag:bool}, derived:{flag:bool}}; per-node vendorExtensions:{vendor:any} escape hatch. This schema is directly modeled on the Crestron JSON's own vocabulary of Type/Info/Transformations/Next.
findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json top-level keys: SchemaVersion, GeneralInformation, UserAttributes, Transports, SupportedFeatures, CommandIds, Commands, Responses, Conditions, Transformations, Rules, Controllers, InputOutput
findings.implication: Because Crestron's own format is already close to a superset of Extron's, the IR is best designed as 'Crestron's shape, generalized and given an Extron-shaped compiled leaf state' rather than as a new abstraction invented from scratch — but two of its fields had to be corrected after the 5-command walkthrough (see next two findings).

findings.claim: Template composability confirmed byte-for-byte: Crestron's SetVolume is a Template whose parent is Packet (Values.Function='{:hex} 01 00 00 {Volume}'), Packet's parent is PacketWithCheckSum (Values.Body='{:hex} 08 22 {Function}'), and PacketWithCheckSum applies a CheckSum transform (Twos complement) over {Body} then an AsByte (UIntToLittleEndianBytes,Operand=1) transform to serialize it — a two-level template chain plus a two-step transform pipeline. Extron's self.build(cmd1,cmd2,cmd3,value) (a single hand-written function) computes checksum = bytes([(~sum(command_string)&0xFF)+1]) over pack('6B',0x08,0x22,cmd1,cmd2,cmd3,value) — the identical twos-complement-of-sum algorithm over the identical 6 leading bytes.
findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json Commands[name=SetVolume/Packet/PacketWithCheckSum], Transformations[name=CheckSum,AsByte]; controlscript .py lines 43-48, 201-205
findings.implication: IR's Template node must support parent-chaining with a Values map (not just a flat command string) precisely because that is the only representation that lets one Checksum transform definition serve every command in the driver instead of being re-derived per command — Extron's version inlines the same computation as a single shared helper method, so both sides already independently converged on 'factor the framing out once.'

findings.claim: SCHEMA CORRECTION #1 (found via testing SetVolume against both Crestron transports): Command.templateRef cannot be a single flat field — it must be transport-scoped. Crestron's Serial SetVolume binds to Packet/PacketWithCheckSum (binary, checksum-framed). Crestron's own IP SetVolume for the SAME logical command binds to an entirely different template family: Info.CommandName='RpcRequest', Values={'params':'"volume":"{Volume}"','method':'directVolumeControl'}, over an HttpTransport posting JSON to https://{_Host_}:{_Port_} with Content-Type application/json — no checksum, no binary framing, no shared bytes with Serial's version at all.
findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/IP_embedded_driver.json Transports[0] (Type:Http, Url template, ContentType application/json) and Commands[name=SetVolume] (Info.CommandName='RpcRequest', Values.method='directVolumeControl'); contrast with Serial_embedded_driver.json Commands[name=SetVolume]
findings.implication: A single IR Command object needs Command.templateBindings:{transportRef→templateRef} (and transformSteps may also need to be transport-scoped), not one templateRef. This is direct evidence from Crestron's own two transports disagreeing with each other on the SAME logical command, not a hypothetical.

findings.claim: Extron's own precedent for 'one logical driver, N transports' is per-transport SUBCLASS DUPLICATION, not per-transport template selection inside one shared command table: SerialClass(SerialInterface, DeviceClass) and SerialOverEthernetClass(EthernetClientInterface, DeviceClass) both instantiate the identical DeviceClass (same Commands dict, same build() framing, same regex matchers) — the .pkp packages this as 12 DriverModelAsset entries (6 distinct model names × 2), each carrying the same _scriptFileName/_scriptClassName pointing at the one embedded smsg_10_6738.py, and each with its own SerialProtocolAsset or EthernetProtocolAsset (7 of each in class_instance_counts).
findings.evidence: controlscript .py lines 388-419 (class SerialClass / class SerialOverEthernetClass); pkp/smsg_10_6738_v1_0_0.pkp resolved via tools/pkp_dump.py: 12 DriverModelAsset objects (ids 110-121) resolving to names ['QN43LS03DAFXZA','QN43LS03DAFXZA','QN50LS03DAFXZA',...] (6 names ×2), class_instance_counts SerialProtocolAsset:7, EthernetProtocolAsset:7
findings.implication: Extron's transport-portability strategy is 'the wire encoding never changes across transports, only the socket layer does' (true here because the frame is checksum-guarded binary either way) — which is why one script serves two Extron transports untouched, whereas Crestron needed genuinely different templates for its two transports because IP moved to a JSON-RPC-over-HTTP wire protocol instead of reusing the serial frame. The IR's Transport abstraction has to support both cases: same templateBindings across transports (Extron-style, common case) and per-transport-divergent templateBindings (Crestron-style, when the vendor changed wire protocol along with the socket).

findings.claim: TEST 1 — SetVolume(50) round-trips cleanly both directions. IR: Command SetVolume{param:VolumePercent(integer,0,100,1,'%'), templateBindings:{serial:'Packet'}, transformSteps:[{AsByte,'{Volume}','Volume'}]}, plus the shared Packet/PacketWithCheckSum/CheckSum/AsByte templates and transforms above. IR→Crestron: emits verbatim what is already in Serial_embedded_driver.json (no lossy step). IR→Extron: codegen recognizes the common two-level template shape (Packet⊂PacketWithCheckSum with a Twos-complement Checksum over the body) and collapses it to the exact self.build(cmd1,cmd2,cmd3,value) helper Extron already hand-wrote, then emits 'VolumeCmdString = self.build(0x01,0x00,0x00,int(value))' guarded by the ParamDef's 0<=value<=100 range check.
findings.evidence: controlscript .py lines 201-205 ('if 0 <= value <= 100: VolumeCmdString = self.build(0x01, 0x00, 0x00, int(value))'); tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json Commands[SetVolume]
findings.implication: This is the clean case: no representational leak because both vendors already independently encode identical bytes for identical semantics, and the IR's Template/Transform primitives are expressive enough to regenerate both source forms exactly.

findings.claim: TEST 2 — SetInput('HDMI 2') round-trips with a naming/shape leak but no byte leak. Extron: ValueStateValues['HDMI 2']=(0x05,0x01) fed as two positional args into build(0x0A,0x00,0x05,0x01). Crestron: MapInputsToCommandString maps 'Hdmi2'→'\x05\x01' (one 2-byte string) substituted into Function='{:hex} 0a 00 {ConvertedInput}' — identical 4 resulting bytes (0A 00 05 01). IR represents the value transform as one Map transform producing a multi-byte blob (Crestron's shape); IR→Extron codegen must mechanically split that blob back into two positional build() arguments, which is a straightforward unpacking, not a semantic loss.
findings.evidence: controlscript .py lines 97-108 (SetInput ValueStateValues dict of 2-tuples, build(0x0A,0x00,val[0],val[1])); tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json Transformations[name=MapInputsToCommandString] and Commands[name=SetVideoInput]
findings.implication: IR's Map transform output type must be 'raw byte string of variable length', and the Extron code-generator needs a template-introspection step that knows how many trailing template placeholders a Map's output should be split across — a small but real asymmetry in how the two vendor source forms spell the same 2-byte substitution.

findings.claim: TEST 2b — a genuine one-sided naming leak: Crestron's outer capability manifest declares SupportsSetAudioInputSource/SupportsAudioInputFeedback:true under the 'Inputs' feature, but no 'SetAudioInput'/'GetAudioInput' command exists anywhere in the Serial driver's 50 Commands (full list enumerated: PacketWithCheckSum, Packet, SetVolume, GetVolume, SetPower, SetPowerOn, GetChannel, GetPower, Select, Exit, Menu, Home, GetVideoInput, SetVideoInput, SetMediaService, ToggleMute, GetMute, Play, Stop, Pause, Back, ChannelUp, ChannelDown, SetChannel, Guide, Up, Down, Left, Right, 10×Keypress*, Red, Green, Blue, Yellow, SetArtwork, SetVideoConfiguration, GetVideoConfiguration, AmbientOn, AmbientOff — no audio-input command among them).
findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/Serial/FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial.dat features list entry SupportsSetAudioInputSource:true; tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json Commands (all 50 names enumerated, none named *AudioInput*)
findings.implication: A declared capability flag is not proof a command exists to back it — this is exactly why the IR's CapabilitySet should be a DERIVED projection (computed from which Commands/Controllers actually exist) rather than trusting either vendor's own declared flag list as ground truth.

findings.claim: TEST 3 — SetPower('On') reveals the biggest asymmetry: Crestron's SetPower Function template is '{:hex} 00 00 00 {Power}' with MapPowerCommands{false:'\x01', true:'\x02'} — so read literally, 'true' would encode as bytes 00 00 00 02. But that is NOT what reaches the wire for On: Extron's own On encoding is build(0x0D,0x00,0x00,0x02) = 0D 00 00 02 (cmd1=0x0D, not 0x00), and Crestron matches this only because Rule 'SendPowerOn' (AppliesTo:SetPower, Condition:PowerIsOn, Type:CommandSequence) intercepts and substitutes an entirely different Command, SetPowerOn, whose Function is the fixed literal '{:hex} 0D 00 00 02' with no substitution at all. SetPower's own true-branch mapping is therefore dead/unreachable in practice — a real, non-obvious artifact only visible by tracing the Rule engine.
findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json Commands[name=SetPower].Info.Values.Function, Commands[name=SetPowerOn].Info.Values.Function; Transformations[name=MapPowerCommands]; Rules[name=SendPowerOn]; controlscript .py lines 172-181 (SetPower ValueStateValues={'On':(0x0D,0x02),'Off':(0x00,0x01)})
findings.implication: SCHEMA CORRECTION #2: a Command's params can select an entirely different wire template, not just a byte value inside one shared template — Extron represents this natively as a dict-of-2-tuples inside one Python function (cmd1 varies with direction), so the IR needs Command.valueTemplateMap:{value:templateRef} as a first-class alternative to Crestron's own Rule+CommandSequence detour. The IR can be MORE explicit here than either vendor source: Extron already has the right shape (in-language dispatch), Crestron buries the same fact in an unrelated regex-matched Rule object.

findings.claim: TEST 3b — warm-up/cool-down state machinery is present and load-bearing on the Crestron side and structurally absent — not just unused — on the Extron side. Crestron: Controllers[WarmUp]={Type:TimedStatus,Timeout:5000ms}, Controllers[CoolDown]={Timeout:3000ms}; Rules WarmUpBlockSend/CoolDownBlockSend block ALL commands except GetPower while WarmingUp/CoolingDown is true; Rules StartWarmUpWithCommand/StartCoolDownWithCommand set those states on SetPowerOn/SetPower sends; both SetPower and SetPowerOn carry PostCommandDelay:2000(ms). Extron: grepping the full .pkp DriverCommandAsset for 'Power' (id 104, and its 12 per-model duplicates) shows its only fields are CommandPacing (unset/None), PollingInterval (=3, i.e. 3s, used only for periodic feedback refresh), _exCmdId and description/name fields — no timeout, no post-command-delay, no block/holdoff concept anywhere in either the .py module (no Wait() calls, no state-machine fields on DeviceClass) or the .pkp asset schema itself.
findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json Controllers[name=WarmUp/CoolDown], Rules[name=WarmUpBlockSend/CoolDownBlockSend/StartWarmUpWithCommand/StartCoolDownWithCommand], Commands[SetPower/SetPowerOn].PostCommandDelay=2000; pkp/smsg_10_6738_v1_0_0.pkp via tools/pkp_dump.py: DriverCommandAsset id=104 name='Power' member keys = {AssetBase+_name, CommandAssetBase+_scriptName, CommandPacing(None), PollingInterval(=3), _exCmdId, _extronName, ...} — no PostCommandDelay/Timeout/Warmup/Cooldown field present; controlscript .py entire file has zero calls to extronlib.system.Wait despite importing it (line 4)
findings.implication: This is the design's hardest case: IR→Crestron for Controllers/Rules/PostCommandDelay is lossless (native target), but IR→Extron is LOSSY BY CONSTRUCTION unless the code generator synthesizes brand-new imperative Python (a Wait()-driven guard flag around Send calls) that has no equivalent construct anywhere in Extron's own driver grammar to decompile back from — meaning round-tripping Extron output back through the IR a second time would silently lose the warm-up/cool-down guarantee again unless the generator's synthesized code is itself tagged with an IR provenance comment. Name what the IR cannot represent: it can describe the guard, but it cannot guarantee an Extron consumer enforces it, because Extron's runtime model has no primitive for 'block send while state X is true' — only vendor firmware-level PollingInterval and CommandPacing knobs, which are the wrong tool (they govern polling cadence and inter-command spacing, not power-state gating).

findings.claim: TEST 4 — GetVolume/UpdateVolume (polling) round-trips but the polling-interval metadata lives in structurally different homes per vendor, both outside the wire encoding itself. Crestron: Controllers[name=Volume].PollingInterval=4000 (ms) sits inline in the same JSON as the Commands/Responses. Extron: the .pkp's DriverCommandAsset for 'Volume' (and its 12 per-model duplicates) carries PollingInterval resolving to a DecimalParamAsset with value=3 (i.e. 3s) — but this field is NOT in the runtime .py at all; UpdateVolume() (lines 209-212) is a pure byte-builder with no timing logic, and the actual poll cadence is enforced by the Global Configurator processor firmware reading the .pkp asset, external to the script.
findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json Controllers[name=Volume].PollingInterval=4000; pkp/smsg_10_6738_v1_0_0.pkp via tools/pkp_dump.py: DriverCommandAsset id=100 name='Volume', PollingInterval→DecimalParamAsset value='3' (13 total instances, one per model/transport duplicate); controlscript .py lines 209-212 (UpdateVolume has no Wait/timing)
findings.implication: IR Controller.pollingIntervalMs is representable losslessly for both vendors, but the code generator must know it routes to two different artifacts: inline JSON for Crestron, a separate .pkp DriverCommandAsset for Extron — the IR schema itself doesn't need a vendor branch here, only the codegen/serializer does. Also note the two vendors independently chose different intervals for the same signal (4000ms vs 3000ms) — the IR should store the value once and let per-target overrides be explicit if a real conversion ever needs to preserve vendor-specific tuning rather than picking one arbitrarily.

findings.claim: TEST 5 — one-sided command: SetArtwork/AmbientOn/AmbientOff exist only on the Crestron side and use the SAME Packet/PacketWithCheckSum/Checksum machinery as every other command (Function='{:hex} 0b 0b 0e {Artwork}' with MapBoolAs01, and two fixed-literal companions '{:hex} 0b 0b 10 01'/'...10 00'). Extron's Commands dict (py lines 25-35: ConnectionStatus, AspectRatio, AudioMute, ChannelStep, Input, Keypad, MenuNavigation, Power, Volume) has no Artwork/Ambient concept at all, and no method (SetArtwork/etc.) exists anywhere in the 429-line module.
findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json Commands[name=SetArtwork/AmbientOn/AmbientOff]; controlscript .py lines 25-35 (self.Commands dict, 9 keys, no Artwork key)
findings.implication: This is a coverage gap, not a representational one — the IR's Template/Transform primitives handle SetArtwork trivially (it's structurally identical to every other command). The IR must therefore let a Command's per-vendor-binding set be a strict subset (Command.vendorBindings:{crestron:{...}, extron:null}) rather than assuming every canonical command has bindings on every target; generating Extron output simply omits the method, which is correct behavior, not data loss, though the underlying physical feature (Art Mode) genuinely becomes inaccessible through that vendor's control surface — the IR can expose that gap but cannot close it.

findings.claim: Capability taxonomy: Crestron's deviceTypeId ('FlatPanelDisplay') plus a fixed 63-entry Supports* boolean list is a real, first-party fixed vocabulary used by Crestron's own UI/programming tools (SIMPL) to gate which controls appear; Extron's package format has no analogous top-level taxonomy object at all — GC infers capability by which Set*/Update* methods exist on DeviceClass (structural/duck-typed), and the closest Extron analog to a 'flag' is the DriverCommandAsset.PollingInterval/CommandPacing pair, which is per-command metadata, not a device-level feature flag.
findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/Serial/FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial.dat: deviceTypeId='FlatPanelDisplay', features (len=63) e.g. {'id':'SupportsCoolDownTime','value':true}, {'id':'SupportsWarmUpTime','value':true}; controlscript .py lines 25-35 (self.Commands dict is the only capability-adjacent structure, keyed by command name with empty {'Status':{}} placeholders, no boolean flags)
findings.implication: The IR needs a CapabilitySet, but it should not be owned by either vendor: (1) treat 'declared' flags (as authored, possibly aspirational per the audio-input finding above) as separate from 'derived' flags computed structurally from which Commands/Controllers/params actually exist in the IR document — Extron output is entirely representable via the derived half even though it never declares anything; (2) keep the flag-name vocabulary itself as an open, versioned, extensible set seeded from Crestron's 63 names (since it's the only mature vocabulary observed) but not literally scoped to Crestron's namespace, so a future vendor's undeclarable-elsewhere feature can add a new flag rather than being forced into VendorExtensions.

findings.claim: Vendor-specific escape hatch is needed for at least: (a) Crestron's DLL wrapper metadata (class name 'Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Legacy.<name>_dll', 'Type':'Simpl' in the JSON) which is packaging/runtime-shell information with no IR equivalent; (b) Extron's per-model/per-transport .pkp asset duplication mechanics (DriverModelAsset._defaultCmdPacing, _defaultMatchStringBufferSize=1024, _commSheetHelpDoc) which are GC-runtime tuning knobs, not device behavior; (c) Crestron's checksum-validation Condition ('ValidCheckSum': IsEqual{CalculatedCheckSum:{CheckSum}}) which is declared in Conditions but never referenced by any Rule in the Serial driver — i.e. present as dead/reserved metadata; (d) Crestron's SequencedEntry Rule type for multi-keystroke channel entry (UseSequencedEntry, ReplaceChars, SequenceEndCommands) which has no Extron counterpart at all in this sample (Extron's SetChannelStep only does relative up/down, no direct numeric channel entry).
findings.evidence: CLAUDE.md-adjacent session note D on 'Simpl' type and LegacyWrappers class name (already established); tools/out/crestron/Serial_embedded_driver.json Conditions[name=ValidCheckSum] (present, unreferenced by any Rules[] entry); Rules[name=UseSequencedEntry]; controlscript .py lines 84-95 (SetChannelStep is Up/Down only, no numeric SetChannel)
findings.implication: A per-node vendorExtensions:{vendorName:any} bag is unavoidable and should be treated as normal, not a design failure — packaging/runtime-shell facts (a,b) and legacy/dead metadata (c) are exactly the kind of thing an IR should NOT try to model formally, since doing so would import one vendor's toolchain assumptions into a supposedly neutral format.

openQuestions: Extron's .pkp DriverCommandAsset schema was only sampled for Power/Volume — does any OTHER command in the 154-entry catalog carry a warm-up/cool-down-like field under a different name that this session's ad hoc pkp introspection missed (the parser emits raw NRBF objects, not a documented schema), which would weaken the 'structurally absent' claim?

Is PollingInterval's unit (bare integer '3' vs Crestron's explicit milliseconds '4000') actually seconds on the Extron side, or is this an undocumented GC convention that varies by asset type — worth confirming against the Extron comm-sheet PDF or GC documentation rather than inferring from the numeral alone.

Does the Crestron IP driver (80,877 B, 77 Commands) implement SetArtwork/Ambient* at all, or is Art-Mode control itself IP-only within Crestron's own family — if so, 'Crestron has it, Extron doesn't' would actually be 'Crestron-IP has it, Crestron-Serial and Extron-both don't', changing the one-sided-command narrative from a vendor split to a transport split.

For the value-dependent whole-template-selection case (SetPower/SetPowerOn), does Extron's comm sheet PDF document any device-side behavior if the 'wrong' encoding (00 00 00 02) were sent, which would confirm SetPower's own true-branch mapping is genuinely dead/unreachable in Crestron rather than a redundant-but-harmless second path.

Should CommandIds' MonotonicIntegerId (Crestron's per-driver-instance transaction/ack-correlation counter, Min 1 Max 127) be modeled as a first-class IR construct given Extron's driver has no visible per-command-instance ID at the wire level (only a fixed checksum) — is that a genuine protocol-level difference or purely a Crestron SDK bookkeeping artifact never sent on the wire?
